title: Leaders Who Criticize Character
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note warns that deeply disappointed leaders can slip from criticizing behavior into criticizing character. Calling someone irresponsible rather than naming the late notice of a changed deadline threatens the person's identity and tends to provoke defensiveness, disengagement, or retaliation. The note identifies 'you always', 'you never', and 'you are' as reliable signs that judgment of a person has replaced feedback on behavior. It offers a memorable test: before criticizing, ask whether a video camera could have recorded what you are about to describe, since a camera can capture lateness but not laziness. The underlying rationale is that behavior can be changed while character is far more fixed. The piece closes with the maxim that the best leaders hold people fully accountable while leaving their sense of self intact, criticizing the play rather than the player.
points: Character criticism threatens identity, producing defensiveness at best and withdrawal or inflammatory retaliation at worst.
Phrases like 'you always', 'you never', and 'you are' signal that a verdict on the person has replaced feedback on behavior.
The video camera test asks whether a criticism describes something observable, like arriving late, rather than a label like irresponsible.
Naming specific actions and their consequences gives team members something concrete they can fix.
quotes: When leaders criticize character, they threaten the self-identity of those on the receiving end. At best, this makes the other person highly defensive. At worst, the team member disengages, withdraws, or lashes back with inflammatory language.

Instead, they make specific observations about what the team member did and why it needs to be corrected. Naming specific actions and the consequences they created gives team members something they can actually address or fix.
Here’s a clever way to prevent character critique. Before offering criticism, leaders should ask whether a video camera could have recorded what they are about to describe.
If a camera can’t capture a leader’s criticism, the leader likely needs to change the focus of their comments.

Leaders must always remember that behavior can be changed, while character is much more fixed. When leaders name what someone did, they invite reflection and improvement. When they name who someone is, they invite a fight or a retreat.
The best leaders hold people fully accountable for their actions while leaving their sense of self intact. They criticize the play, not the player.
